hints: Compare the downslope weight components: for $B$, $1.2g\sin 60^\circ = 12 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 6\sqrt{3} \approx 10.39\text{ N}$, and for $A$, $0.8g\sin 30^\circ = 8 \times 0.5 = 4\text{ N}$. Since $6\sqrt{3} > 4$, $B$ accelerates down its plane and $A$ accelerates up its plane.
Write Newton's second law for particle $A$ moving up its $30^\circ$ plane: $T - 0.8g\sin 30^\circ = 0.8a \implies T - 4 = 0.8a$.
Write Newton's second law for particle $B$ moving down its $60^\circ$ plane: $1.2g\sin 60^\circ - T = 1.2a \implies 6\sqrt{3} - T = 1.2a$.

Add the two equations to eliminate $T$ and find $a = \frac{6\sqrt{3}-4}{2} = 3\sqrt{3}-2 \approx 3.20\text{ m s}^{-2}$, then substitute $a$ back to obtain $T = \frac{12}{5}(1+\sqrt{3}) \approx 6.56\text{ N}$.
walkthrough:
Compare the downslope gravitational force components for both particles to find the direction of acceleration:
$$W_{A,\text{slope}} = m_A g \sin 30^\circ = 0.8 \times 10 \times 0.5 = 4\text{ N}$$
$$W_{B,\text{slope}} = m_B g \sin 60^\circ = 1.2 \times 10 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 6\sqrt{3} \approx 10.3923\text{ N}$$
Because $10.3923 > 4$, particle $B$ moves down its incline and pulls particle $A$ up its incline with common acceleration magnitude $a$.

State Newton's second law $F_{\text{net}} = ma$ along the line of greatest slope for particle $A$ moving upwards:
$$T - m_A g \sin 30^\circ = m_A a$$
$$T - 4 = 0.8a \quad \text{--- (Equation 1)}$$

State Newton's second law along the line of greatest slope for particle $B$ moving downwards:
$$m_B g \sin 60^\circ - T = m_B a$$
$$6\sqrt{3} - T = 1.2a \quad \text{--- (Equation 2)}$$

Add Equation 1 and Equation 2 to eliminate the internal tension $T$:
$$(T - 4) + (6\sqrt{3} - T) = 0.8a + 1.2a$$
$$6\sqrt{3} - 4 = 2a$$

Divide both sides by $2$ to isolate $a$:
$$a = \frac{6\sqrt{3} - 4}{2} = 3\sqrt{3} - 2\text{ m s}^{-2}$$
Evaluate numerically:
$$3\sqrt{3} - 2 \approx 3(1.73205) - 2 = 5.19615 - 2 = 3.19615\text{ m s}^{-2} \approx 3.20\text{ m s}^{-2} \text{ (to 3 s.f.)}$$

Substitute the exact expression for $a$ back into Equation 1 to find tension $T$:
$$T = 4 + 0.8(3\sqrt{3} - 2)$$

Evaluate $T$ to 3 significant figures:
$$T = 2.4(1 + 1.73205) = 2.4(2.73205) = 6.55692\text{ N} \approx 6.56\text{ N}$$

hints: At limiting equilibrium, identify impending motion: $B$ tends to move down its $60^\circ$ plane while $A$ tends to move up its $30^\circ$ plane, so friction opposes both directions.
Calculate normal reactions perpendicular to the planes: $R_A = 0.8g\cos 30^\circ = 4\sqrt{3}\text{ N}$ and $R_B = 1.2g\cos 60^\circ = 6\text{ N}$.
Express limiting friction on each plane: $F_A = \mu R_A = 4\sqrt{3}\mu$ (acting down $A$'s slope) and $F_B = \mu R_B = 6\mu$ (acting up $B$'s slope).
Set up the equilibrium equation for the entire system along the string: $1.2g\sin 60^\circ - 0.8g\sin 30^\circ - F_A - F_B = 0$, and solve for $\mu$.
walkthrough: Identify the impending motion of the system: because the downslope weight component of $B$ ($6\sqrt{3}\text{ N}$) exceeds that of $A$ ($4\text{ N}$), the impending motion is for $B$ to slide down its plane and $A$ to be pulled up its plane.
Determine the directions of limiting friction: friction on $B$ acts up its plane (opposing descent), and friction on $A$ acts down its plane (opposing ascent).

Calculate the normal reactions perpendicular to each plane:
$$R_A = m_A g \cos 30^\circ = 0.8 \times 10 \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} = 4\sqrt{3}\text{ N}$$
$$R_B = m_B g \cos 60^\circ = 1.2 \times 10 \times 0.5 = 6\text{ N}$$

Apply the limiting friction formula $F = \mu R$ to both particles:
$$F_A = \mu R_A = 4\sqrt{3}\mu$$
$$F_B = \mu R_B = 6\mu$$

Write the equilibrium equation along the slope for particle $A$:
$$T - m_A g \sin 30^\circ - F_A = 0 \implies T - 4 - 4\sqrt{3}\mu = 0 \implies T = 4 + 4\sqrt{3}\mu$$

Write the equilibrium equation along the slope for particle $B$:
$$m_B g \sin 60^\circ - F_B - T = 0 \implies 6\sqrt{3} - 6\mu - T = 0 \implies T = 6\sqrt{3} - 6\mu$$

Equate the two expressions for tension $T$ to eliminate $T$:
$$4 + 4\sqrt{3}\mu = 6\sqrt{3} - 6\mu$$

Collect all terms containing $\mu$ on the left side and constant terms on the right side:
$$4\sqrt{3}\mu + 6\mu = 6\sqrt{3} - 4$$
$$(6 + 4\sqrt{3})\mu = 6\sqrt{3} - 4$$

Divide both sides by $(6 + 4\sqrt{3})$ to isolate $\mu$:
$$\mu = \frac{6\sqrt{3} - 4}{6 + 4\sqrt{3}}$$

Compute the numerator and denominator using $\sqrt{3} \approx 1.73205$:
$$\text{Numerator} = 6(1.73205) - 4 = 10.3923 - 4 = 6.3923$$
$$\text{Denominator} = 6 + 4(1.73205) = 6 + 6.9282 = 12.9282$$
$$\mu = \frac{6.3923}{12.9282} \approx 0.49444 = 0.494 \text{ (to 3 s.f.)}$$
